title: Council at Jerusalem
summary: Apostles and elders decided that Gentile believers need not be circumcised. It is the New Testament's model for church councils, though it isn't counted among the ecumenical councils.

title: Fire of Rome and Nero's persecution
summary: Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome, the first known persecution by the Roman state. Early tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in this period.

title: Destruction of Jerusalem
summary: Roman forces destroyed the city and the Temple, which ended Temple sacrifice and sped the separation of church and synagogue.

title: Marcion's break with the Roman church
summary: Marcion rejected the Old Testament and kept a shortened New Testament of Luke and Paul. His movement was condemned, and scholars debate how far it pushed the church to define its own canon.

title: The Gnostic challenge
summary: Gnostic teachers offered secret knowledge and a lower creator god. Answering them shaped early appeals to apostolic succession, the rule of faith and the canon.

title: Montanism
summary: The New Prophecy of Montanus in Phrygia claimed new revelation and stricter discipline. It was rejected by church synods, though Tertullian joined it.

title: The rule of faith in Irenaeus and Tertullian
summary: Writers summarized apostolic teaching in a short rule of faith, an early form of the later creeds.

title: Muratorian list of New Testament books
summary: An early list of accepted Christian writings, usually dated to the late second century, though some scholars date it later.

title: Tertullian's Trinitarian language
summary: Against Praxeas, Tertullian used the Latin trinitas and spoke of one substance in three persons, wording that shaped later Western theology.
quote: from the Lat. trinitas, first used by Tertullian (A.D. 220)

title: Decian persecution and the lapsed
summary: The first empire-wide persecution required public sacrifice. Whether to restore those who gave in divided the church.

title: Novatian schism
summary: Novatian formed a rival church at Rome that refused to restore those who lapsed under persecution.

title: Diocletian's persecution
summary: The last and severest Roman persecution ordered churches destroyed and Scriptures surrendered.

title: Constantine and the Edict of Milan
summary: Christianity became a tolerated religion in the Roman Empire, and the church's relation to the state began to change.

title: Donatist schism
summary: North African Christians split over clergy who had surrendered Scriptures under persecution. Augustine's answer shaped Western teaching on the church and sacraments.

title: Arian controversy begins
summary: Arius of Alexandria taught that the Son was created and had a beginning, which set off the central Trinitarian debate of the fourth century.

title: First Council of Nicaea
summary: The first council counted as ecumenical. It rejected Arianism and confessed the Son as homoousios, of one substance with the Father.

title: Athanasius's list of the 27 New Testament books
summary: His Easter letter of 367 is the earliest known list naming exactly the 27 books of today's New Testament.

title: Christianity made the imperial religion
summary: Theodosius I ordered his subjects to hold the Nicene faith, and Christianity became the religion of the empire.

title: First Council of Constantinople
summary: Reaffirmed Nicaea and affirmed the Holy Spirit's deity. The creed recited today as the Nicene Creed is linked with this council.

title: Jerome's Latin Bible
summary: Jerome's translation, later called the Vulgate, became the Bible of the medieval West. He preferred the Hebrew text for the Old Testament.

title: Pelagian controversy
summary: Augustine and Pelagius disputed sin, free will and grace. Pelagius's teaching was condemned, and Augustine's teaching on grace shaped Western theology.

title: Sack of Rome and Augustine's City of God
summary: The Goths sacked Rome in 410. Augustine answered pagan blame for it with The City of God, a lasting Christian account of history.

title: Council of Ephesus
summary: Condemned Nestorius and affirmed Mary as Theotokos, God-bearer. The Church of the East doesn't accept this council.

title: The Robber Council of Ephesus
summary: A disputed synod backed Eutyches and was later set aside at Chalcedon. Leo the Great gave it the name "Robber Synod."

title: Council of Chalcedon
summary: Defined Christ as one person in two natures, without confusion or division. Oriental Orthodox churches don't accept it.

title: Churches divide over Chalcedon
summary: The Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and related churches separated from those accepting Chalcedon. They reject the label Monophysite and prefer miaphysite.

title: Council of Orange
summary: A regional council in Gaul rejected semi-Pelagianism and affirmed the need of grace from the beginning of faith.

title: The Rule of Benedict
summary: Benedict of Nursia's rule for Monte Cassino became the pattern of Western monastic life.

title: Second Council of Constantinople
summary: Condemned the Three Chapters in an attempt to reconcile those who rejected Chalcedon. It didn't heal the division.

title: Filioque at the Council of Toledo
summary: The Spanish church's creed at Toledo included "and the Son," a Western addition that became a main dispute with the East.

title: Papacy of Gregory the Great
summary: Gregory strengthened the Roman see, sent a mission to England and shaped medieval pastoral practice.

title: Rise of Islam
summary: Arab conquests took the Christian lands of Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa, and reshaped the church's geography.

title: Third Council of Constantinople
summary: Rejected Monotheletism and confessed two wills in Christ, following Maximus the Confessor's teaching.

title: The iconoclastic controversy begins
summary: Byzantine emperors moved against religious images, which divided the Eastern church for more than a century.

title: Second Council of Nicaea
summary: Restored the veneration of images and distinguished it from worship. Protestants generally don't accept this council.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: The pope crowned Charlemagne in Rome, which tied the Western church to a new empire and widened the distance from Constantinople.

title: Final restoration of images in the East
summary: Images were restored for good in the East, an event the Orthodox still mark as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

title: Gottschalk and the predestination dispute
summary: The monk Gottschalk taught double predestination and was condemned, in a controversy later cited in Reformation debates.

title: Photian schism
summary: Pope Nicholas and Patriarch Photius excommunicated each other in a dispute over authority and the Filioque.

title: The monastery of Cluny
summary: Cluny's independence from lay control became the base of a broad monastic reform.

title: East-West Schism
summary: Rome's legates and Patriarch Cerularius excommunicated each other at Constantinople. Historians see this as one stage in a longer separation.

title: Investiture conflict and Canossa
summary: Emperor Henry IV sought absolution from Gregory VII at Canossa, in the struggle over who appointed bishops.

title: First Crusade
summary: Urban II's call at Clermont led to the capture of Jerusalem, with lasting effects on relations with Muslims, Jews and Eastern Christians.

title: Anselm's Cur Deus Homo
summary: Anselm explained the atonement as satisfaction for the honor owed to God, a turning point in Western thinking on the cross.

title: Concordat of Worms
summary: A compromise over the investiture of bishops between Pope Callistus II and Emperor Henry V.

title: The Waldensian movement
summary: Peter Waldo's followers preached poverty and the Scriptures in the common tongue, and were condemned. The Waldensian church survives today.

title: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
summary: Crusaders captured and sacked the Eastern capital, which hardened the division between East and West.

title: Franciscans and Dominicans
summary: New mendicant orders brought preaching and poverty to the growing towns of Europe.

title: Fourth Lateran Council
summary: Under Innocent III it used the word transubstantiation in a conciliar decree and required yearly confession. Catholics count it as ecumenical.

title: Papal Inquisition organized
summary: Church courts were organized to prosecute heresy, with force supplied by civil rulers.

title: Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica
summary: Aquinas brought Aristotle's philosophy into a large synthesis of Christian theology, the height of scholasticism.

title: Unam Sanctam
summary: Boniface VIII's bull made one of the strongest medieval claims for papal authority.

title: The papacy at Avignon
summary: The popes lived at Avignon in France for nearly seventy years, which damaged their standing across Europe.

title: Western Schism
summary: Rival popes, at one point three, divided Western Europe until the Council of Constance ended the split.

title: Wyclif and the English Bible
summary: John Wyclif challenged papal claims and transubstantiation, and inspired an English translation of the Bible.

title: Council of Constance and the burning of Hus
summary: The council ended the Western Schism, asserted its own authority and condemned John Hus, who was burned in 1415.

title: Council of Ferrara-Florence
summary: Greek and Latin delegates signed a union of the churches, including the Filioque. Most in the East rejected it.

title: Fall of Constantinople
summary: The Ottoman capture ended the Byzantine Empire and placed the Eastern patriarchate under Ottoman rule.

title: Erasmus's Greek New Testament
summary: The first published Greek New Testament, the root of the Textus Receptus behind the KJV and other Reformation Bibles.

title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: Luther's challenge to the sale of indulgences is usually taken as the start of the Protestant Reformation.

title: Diet of Worms
summary: Luther refused to recant before Charles V and was outlawed, after the pope had excommunicated him.

title: Reformation in Zurich
summary: Zwingli's Sixty-seven Articles led to Zurich's break with Rome and the beginning of the Reformed tradition.

title: Anabaptists begin in Zurich
summary: Conrad Grebel and others began baptizing believers. Their movement was persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike.

title: Schleitheim Confession
summary: The first known Anabaptist confession, covering believers' baptism, separation from the world, and the refusal of arms and oaths.

title: Marburg Colloquy
summary: Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen articles but not on Christ's presence in the Supper, which left the two Protestant streams apart.

title: Augsburg Confession
summary: Melanchthon's statement of Lutheran faith, presented to Charles V, and still the chief Lutheran confession.

title: English church breaks with Rome
summary: Parliament's Act of Supremacy made Henry VIII head of the Church of England.

title: Calvin's Institutes
summary: Calvin's first edition appeared at Basel. Expanded through 1559, it became the classic statement of Reformed theology.

title: Calvin returns to Geneva
summary: Calvin's church order in Geneva became a model for Reformed churches across Europe.

title: Council of Trent
summary: The Catholic answer to the Reformation defined Scripture and tradition, justification and the seven sacraments, and reformed church discipline.

title: Consensus of Zurich
summary: Calvin and Bullinger agreed on the Lord's Supper, which united the Swiss Reformed streams.

title: Peace of Augsburg
summary: German princes could choose between Lutheran and Catholic faith for their lands. Reformed and Anabaptist Christians were left out.

title: Scots Confession
summary: John Knox and others wrote this confession as Scotland adopted the Reformation.

title: Belgic Confession
summary: Written for the persecuted churches of the Low Countries, it became a standard of Dutch Reformed churches.

title: Heidelberg Catechism
summary: Prepared for the Palatinate, it became one of the most widely used Reformed catechisms.

title: Second Helvetic Confession
summary: Bullinger's confession was adopted by the Swiss Reformed churches and widely received abroad.

title: Thirty-Nine Articles
summary: The doctrinal statement of the Church of England, finalized under Elizabeth I.

title: Formula of Concord
summary: Settled disputes among Lutherans after Luther's death and completed the Lutheran confessions.

title: The Arminian Remonstrance
summary: Followers of Jacob Arminius set out five articles on election, atonement, grace and perseverance.

title: Synod of Dort
summary: A Reformed synod with delegates from several countries rejected the Remonstrance, and its canons are the source of the "five points of Calvinism."

title: Westminster Assembly
summary: The English Parliament called it to reform the Church of England. It produced the Confession and Catechisms, standards of Presbyterian churches.

title: Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila
summary: An Eastern Orthodox statement approved in response to Catholic and Protestant teaching.

title: Peace of Westphalia
summary: The treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War recognized Reformed churches alongside Lutherans and Catholics in the Empire.

title: Savoy Declaration
summary: English Congregationalists adapted the Westminster Confession to their own church order.

title: Synod of Jerusalem and Confession of Dositheus
summary: The Eastern church rejected Calvinist teaching attributed to Patriarch Cyril Lucaris.

title: Spener's Pia Desideria and Pietism
summary: Spener's book set out a program of Bible study, lay participation and practical piety for German Lutherans.

title: The Great Awakening
summary: Revivals under Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield and others spread through the American colonies and Britain.

title: John Wesley at Aldersgate
summary: Wesley's experience on 24 May 1738, hearing Luther's preface to Romans read, is often taken as a beginning of the Methodist movement.
source: Aldersgate SG, The Methodist Church in Singapore
quote: I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation.

title: Schleiermacher's On Religion
summary: Schleiermacher located religion in feeling and intuition, and is often called the father of Protestant liberalism.

title: Dogma of the Immaculate Conception
summary: Pius IX defined that Mary was preserved from original sin at her conception. Orthodox and Protestant churches don't accept this dogma.

title: Syllabus of Errors
summary: Pius IX listed modern ideas the Catholic Church then condemned, including liberalism and rationalism.

title: First Vatican Council
summary: Defined papal primacy and infallibility when the pope speaks ex cathedra on faith and morals. Those who rejected the decree formed the Old Catholic churches.

title: Azusa Street revival
summary: William Seymour's mission in Los Angeles became a main source of the worldwide Pentecostal movement.

title: World Missionary Conference, Edinburgh
summary: Protestant mission leaders met at Edinburgh, in what is often seen as the formal beginning of the ecumenical movement.
source: Musée protestant, “The 1910 World Missionary Conference in Edinburgh”
quote: has been seen as the formal beginning of the Ecumenical movement

title: The Fundamentals
summary: A series of essays against theological liberalism, later seen as a foundation of Christian fundamentalism. The word "Fundamentalist" dates from 1920.

title: Barth's Epistle to the Romans
summary: Dated 1919 and rewritten in 1921, Barth's commentary broke with liberal theology and shaped what became known as neo-orthodoxy.

title: Barmen Declaration
summary: The Confessing Church rejected the Nazi-aligned German Christians. Karl Barth was its major theological influence.

title: World Council of Churches founded
summary: Churches founded the Council on 23 August 1948 at Amsterdam, with 147 churches taking part.

title: Second Vatican Council
summary: Opened by John XXIII and closed by Paul VI, it addressed the church, revelation, liturgy and the modern world, and opened new relations with other Christians.
source: EWTN, “Second Ecumenical Council of the Vatican (1962-1965)”

title: Catholic and Orthodox lift the 1054 excommunications
summary: Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras removed the mutual excommunications of 1054 from memory. Full communion was not restored.

title: Lausanne Covenant
summary: The International Congress on World Evangelization issued a shared evangelical statement on mission.

title: Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy
summary: More than 200 evangelical leaders, at a conference called by the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy, set out the doctrine.

title: Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox agreed statement
summary: At Chambésy, a joint commission produced a shared statement on Christology, addressing the division over Chalcedon.

title: Common Christological Declaration
summary: John Paul II and Mar Dinkha IV of the Assyrian Church of the East affirmed a shared faith in Christ, addressing the division after Ephesus.

title: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification
summary: Lutherans and Catholics signed at Augsburg a shared understanding of basic truths on justification. Methodist, Anglican and Reformed bodies later affirmed it.
source: Lutheran World Federation, “Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification”
